newsitem.title: RUSSIA: ATHLETICS-LASOVSKAYA OUT BUT RUSSIA STILL BUOYANT.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-LASOVSKAYA OUT BUT RUSSIA STILL BUOYANT.

text.p: Russia will be without injured Olympic silver medallist Inna Lasovskaya in the triple jump but are still confident their strong women's entry can assure them overall second place at the world championships in Athens.

Lasovskaya, who jumped an impressive 14.91 metres at the European Cup a month ago, will miss the rest of the season after an Achilles tendon operation in France, athletics federation president Valentin Balakhnichev said on Thursday.
Her loss, the Russians believe, amounts to dropping an all but certain gold medal in the championships starting next week.

But despite the absence of injured sprinter Irina Privalova, several other women including double Olympic champion Svetlana Masterkova, plus pole-vaulter Maxim Tarasov, should win their events, Balakhnichev said.

Tarasov, the 1992 Olympic champion, last week became only the fifth man in history to clear six metres, recording 6.00 in Nice. The only other Russian men with realistic hopes of gold are the 20-km and 50- km walkers.
But Masterkova, winner of the 800 and 1,500 metres at last year's Atlanta Games, leads a strong women's entry that will also stake claims on the 100 and 400 metres relay prizes.

Balakhnichev also cited Tatyana Alexeyeva in the 400 metres and heptathlete Svetlana Moskalets as well as discus thrower Irina Sadovaya and the young high jumper Yulia Lyakhova, who he said had cleared up to 2.04 metres in training this month.
Former world record holder Anna Biryukova will have her chance to come out from Lasovskaya's shadow in the triple jump.

Though harbouring few illusions about Russia's ability to reassert Soviet sporting dominance over the United States, Balakhnichev said Russian athletics was definitely making a comeback from the financial traumas that followed the collapse of communism and should comfortably finish second in Athens.
"Our athletics is on the up due to better financing and equipment, and we will take second place after the Americans," he said. "This will be a step forward.
"It's hard for us to compete with the Americans at the moment. But at the next world championships, with financing improving, we will be a very strong and competitive team."

Equipment sponsorships are now making up for the loss of state funding, he noted, while the draw of up to $60,000 in cash from the IAAF for winning a medal in Athens is big motivation in a country where the average income is about $150 a month.
